summary: The lecture covers the founding of the French East India Company in 1664, its early factories at Surat, Masulipatnam, and Pondicherry, and the Anglo-French Carnatic Wars. The First Carnatic War (1746-48), sparked by the Austrian War of Succession, ended with the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. The Second Carnatic War (1749-54) arose from succession disputes in Hyderabad and Carnatic, featuring Dupleix's diplomacy and Robert Clive's rise, concluding with the Treaty of Pondicherry and British dominance.
points: French East India Company (Compagnie des Indes Orientales) formed in 1664 with 50-year trade monopoly over Pacific and India.
Francis Caron established first French factory at Surat in 1667 with Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb's support.
Francois Martin secured Pondicherry in 1673 from Sher Khan Lodi, governor of Valikandapuram under Bijapur.
Dutch captured Pondicherry in 1697 but returned it under Treaty of Ryswick (1697).
Portuguese introduced tobacco in India; ceded Bombay to England in 1661 as dowry for Catherine of Braganza.
Dutch expelled from India after defeat by Travancore's Marthanda Varma (Battle of Colachel, 1741) led by Ramayyan Dalava.
First Carnatic War (1746-48) began when English ships attacked French fleet; Dupleix and Bourdonnais captured Fort St. George.
Battle of St. Thome (1746): 1,000 French troops defeated 10,000 of Nawab Anwaruddin Khan on Adyar River.
Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) ended First Carnatic War: Louisbourg to France, Fort St. George to English.
Second Carnatic War (1749-54): Dupleix backed Muzaffar Jung and Chanda Sahib; Clive supported Muhammad Ali and Nasir Jung; ended with Treaty of Pondicherry (1754).
